hints: Look at the equation for reaction Z and notice what small molecule is added across sucrose to split it into two smaller sugars.
walkthrough:
Spot what water is doing**
Look at reaction Z: $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow$ glucose + fructose. One large sucrose molecule is being split into two smaller molecules by adding a water molecule. Whenever water splits a larger molecule in this way, chemists give it a special name.
Final answer: hydrolysis

hints: Recall that on a Boltzmann distribution the x-axis is energy and you mark activation energy as a vertical line to the right of the peak.
Think about how a catalyst changes the reaction pathway and whether the new activation energy is higher or lower, while temperature and the shape of the curve stay the same.
Link the area under the curve beyond each activation energy to the proportion of molecules able to react successfully.
walkthrough:
Picture what the curve means**
The y-axis is number of sucrose molecules and the x-axis is energy. The curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak then tails off. The total area under it is all the sucrose molecules. Only those with enough energy to the right of the activation energy line can react when they collide.

Add the two activation energies**
Draw two vertical lines on the energy axis. The one for the uncatalysed reaction, $E_{a}$, is further to the right. The one for the catalysed reaction, $E_{a}(cat)$, is to the left of it, at lower energy. The catalyst provides an alternative route of lower activation energy. The shape of the distribution does not change because temperature is constant.

Compare the areas and explain the rate**
Shade the small tail beyond $E_{a}$ and the larger tail beyond $E_{a}(cat)$. The area beyond $E_{a}(cat)$ is clearly greater. That means a much greater proportion of molecules now have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, so the frequency of successful collisions increases and the reaction is much faster.

Final answer: Mark $E_{a}$ (no catalyst) and $E_{a}(cat)$ at lower energy on energy axis, with $E_{a}(cat) < E_{a}$.
Shade area under curve beyond $E_{a}(cat)$ which is greater than area beyond $E_{a}$.
A greater number / proportion of sucrose molecules have energy $\geq E_{a}(cat)$, so more successful collisions per unit time and faster rate.

hints: Focus on a single carbon atom and count how many different groups must be attached to it to make it chiral.
walkthrough:
Learn the test for chirality**
Picture a carbon with four single bonds sticking out like a tetrahedron. If all four things attached to it are different from each other, that carbon is a chiral centre. It has no plane of symmetry and can exist in two non-superimposable mirror image forms.
Final answer: An atom (usually carbon) bonded to four different atoms / groups / substituents.

hints: Work through the carbon chain of fructose and rule out any carbon that does not have four single bonds, such as $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ carbons.
walkthrough:
Rule out the non-chiral carbons first**
Fructose is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$: $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}-\text{C(=O)}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. The two $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ end carbons each have two identical H atoms, so they cannot be chiral. The $\text{C=O}$ carbon has only three groups joined to it, so it cannot be chiral either.

Confirm the three middle carbons**
Each of the three $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbons in the middle is joined to H, to OH, and to two different chain fragments above and below. That is four different groups in each case, so all three are chiral centres. Mark each of these three carbons with *.

Final answer: Put * on the three central $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbons of fructose: $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{C(=O)C*H(OH)C*H(OH)C*H(OH)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. No * on $\text{C=O}$ or on either $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ carbon.

hints: Count C, H and O atoms in the displayed formula of fructose to get the molecular formula, then divide by the highest common factor.
walkthrough:
Simplify the molecular formula**
From the structure, fructose is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$. The empirical formula is the simplest whole number ratio. Divide all subscripts by 6 to give $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Remember that every standard enthalpy change definition starts with the amount of substance involved, one mole.
Think about what combustion means in terms of burning in oxygen and whether the burning must be complete or incomplete.
walkthrough:
Fix the amount**
Enthalpy change of combustion is always quoted per mole. So start your definition with: when 1 mole of a substance burns.

Fix the conditions of burning**
Combustion means reaction with oxygen to give oxides. For the standard value it must be complete combustion, that is in excess oxygen, so carbon burns fully to $\text{CO}_{2}$ and hydrogen to $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. That gives the full definition.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance burns / combusts completely in oxygen / excess oxygen.

hints: Write the products of complete combustion of a carbohydrate as carbon dioxide and water, then balance C, H and O using sucrose $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$.
walkthrough:
Balance the combustion**
Complete combustion gives $\text{CO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Sucrose has 12 C, so you need $12\text{CO}_{2}$. It has 22 H, so you need $11\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Count O on the right: $(12 \times 2) + 11 = 35$. Sucrose already provides 11 O, so you need 24 more O atoms from $12\text{O}_{2}$. That gives $$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + 12\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 12\text{CO}_{2} + 11\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Draw a Hess cycle with reaction Z ($\text{sucrose} + \text{water} \rightarrow \text{glucose} + \text{fructose}$) on top and all species combusting to $12\text{CO}_{2} + 12\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ below.
Apply $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{c}(\text{reactants}) - \Sigma \Delta H_{c}(\text{products})$, remembering $\Delta H_{c}$ of water is zero and keeping the signs negative.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess cycle**
Draw a triangle. Put sucrose + water going across the top to glucose + fructose, that is $\Delta H_{r}$. Then draw arrows down from both the top left and top right to the same combustion products, $12\text{CO}_{2} + 12\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. By Hess's law, going directly across the top gives the same enthalpy change as going down via combustion of reactants then back up via reverse combustion of products.

Substitute the combustion data**
Water does not burn, so its $\Delta H_{c} = 0$. Using $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{c}(\text{reactants}) - \Sigma \Delta H_{c}(\text{products})$: $$\Delta H_{r} = [-5643 + 0] - [(-2805) + (-2810)]$$ This is $-5643 - (-5615)$.

Calculate the final value**
$-5643 + 5615 = -28$. So $$\Delta H_{r} = -28\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The small negative value shows reaction Z is very slightly exothermic, which makes sense as sucrose, glucose and fructose have very similar combustion enthalpies.

Final answer: Hess cycle showing $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6} + \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$ with combustion arrows down to $12\text{CO}_{2} + 12\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
$$\Delta H_{r} = -5643 - (-2805 + -2810) = -28\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
